opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they kind of reinforce each other.

The first is that most of the mental model around AI risk, both inside companies and in policy, has been built around external deployment. When you release a model to the public, there's a clear moment: there's a launch, there are system cards, there are evaluations, there's press attention, and regulators can point at something. Internal deployment doesn't have that moment. A model just gradually starts being used by more people inside the company, for more tasks, with more permissions, and there's never a single point where someone says, "Okay, now we're deploying this, let's do the full safety review."

The second reason is that the people using the system internally are trusted employees, so there's an intuition that the risk is low. You're not worried about random users trying to jailbreak it to get bioweapons uplift. But that framing misses the risks that matter most for internal deployment. The model itself might be misaligned. It might be scheming. And internally it often has much more access than any external user would ever give it: access to the codebase, to the training infrastructure, sometimes to its own weights or to the next generation of models. If a model were trying to undermine oversight or sabotage safety research, internal deployment is exactly where it would have the most leverage.

Third, there are very strong incentives pushing the other way. The most valuable use of a frontier model for an AI company is often to speed up its own AI research. Every friction you add, like monitoring, restricted permissions, or human review of agent actions, feels like it slows you down in a race where you think a few months matter a lot. And because the benefits are immediate and visible while the risks are speculative and diffuse, it's easy to keep deferring the safeguards.

And finally, there's just not much external pressure. Nobody outside the company sees what's happening internally. There's no customer complaint, no journalist who can test it, and most regulation so far is focused on what gets released to the public. So the normal accountability mechanisms that push companies to take risks seriously mostly don't apply.

Put together, you get this situation where the most capable systems, with the most dangerous affordances, are being used in the least scrutinized setting. That's why I think internal deployment deserves a lot more attention than it currently gets, both from the labs themselves and from governments.

r001.rationale: The response says trusted employees create an intuition that risk is low, but does not identify staff’s subjective sense of control over internal AI as a reason for discounting risk.

r002.rationale: It says safeguards feel like they slow research and conflict with competitive incentives, but does not mention anticipated staff resentment toward costly safeguards.

r003.rationale: The response describes risks as speculative and safeguards as easy to defer, but does not state that staff would view burdensome safeguards as unjustified unless they strongly believed in the risks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of reasons, and I want to be fair to the companies here, because I don't think it's mostly bad intent. I think a lot of it is structural.

The first thing is just that internal deployment is kind of invisible. When you release a model externally, there's a very natural moment where everyone stops and asks, "Is this safe? What could go wrong? What do the evals say?" There are system cards, there's a launch, there's a date. Internal deployment doesn't have that. A model goes from being a research artifact to being a thing that half the company's engineers are using to write code, and there's no single moment where anyone has to make a decision. It's more like a gradient. And it's very hard for organizations to take seriously something that never shows up as a discrete decision.

The second thing is that internally, the people using the system are the people who built it. And so there's this very strong intuition of, "Well, we understand this thing, we trained it, we know what it does." I think that intuition is just wrong, or at least much weaker than people think. We don't really understand these systems. We have evals, we have behavioral evidence, but the thing that makes internal deployment dangerous is precisely that the model has a lot of affordances. It has access to the codebase, it might have access to training infrastructure, it might be writing the code for the next model. So the stakes of a model that's subtly misaligned, or that's scheming, or honestly even just making mistakes in correlated ways, are much higher internally than for a chatbot that's talking to a customer.

And then the third thing, which I think is maybe the most important one, is incentives. The whole point of using your models internally is to go faster. That's the entire value proposition. If I'm a company racing against other companies, and my frontier model can accelerate my research by, let's say, 20% or 50% or whatever the number ends up being, then every safeguard I put on internal deployment feels like I'm giving up some of that speed. And the risk feels abstract and speculative, whereas the speed is extremely concrete. You can measure it. You can see your competitors moving. So the asymmetry is really stark: the costs of being careful show up immediately, and the costs of not being careful show up later, if at all, and are very hard to attribute.

I'd also add that externally, there are other actors who force you to take it seriously. There are regulators, there's the press, there are users who will post screenshots when something goes wrong. Internally, there's none of that. There's basically no external accountability for what you do with your own models inside your own walls. And historically, that's where I'd expect the first really serious incidents to happen — not with the public-facing product, but with the version that's six months ahead and that no one outside the company has ever seen.

So when I talk to people at labs about this, I usually don't find that they disagree with the argument. They mostly nod along. It's more that it's nobody's job, it doesn't have a forcing function, and everyone is very busy. Which is exactly the kind of situation where you'd want some external structure — commitments, reporting, something that makes internal deployment a decision rather than a drift.

r001.rationale: The response says staff who built and use the systems may feel they understand what the systems do, then calls that intuition mistaken.

r002.rationale: It says safeguards feel like giving up speed, but does not identify anticipated staff resentment toward costly safeguards.

r003.rationale: It contrasts abstract risk with concrete speed, but does not state that staff would see burdensome safeguards as justified only if they strongly believed in the risks.

astra-6.text:
I think one difficulty is that internal deployment looks much less like a clear decision point. When you release a model to the public, there’s an obvious moment where you ask: is this safe enough to ship? Internally, you might start by letting it help with coding, then give it access to more tools, then let it run longer tasks. Each step seems useful and fairly small, but collectively you can end up giving the system a lot of access and autonomy.

And the benefits are very concrete. Your researchers are getting more done; your engineers like using it. The risks are harder to demonstrate, especially if you’re worried about a model behaving differently when it has an opportunity to do something harmful. The fact that it’s been helpful so far doesn’t necessarily settle that question.

There’s also a tension in how people think about the boundary of the company. “It’s only internal” sounds reassuring, and in some ways it is: you control who uses it, and you can monitor what happens. But internally is also where your sensitive information and important infrastructure are. So that boundary doesn’t automatically make the consequences small.

Taking those risks seriously means being willing to restrict something that is already making your colleagues more productive, on the basis of evidence that may still be uncertain. That’s a difficult organizational decision, particularly when there’s pressure to move quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says that “it’s only internal” sounds reassuring because the company controls access and can monitor use, identifying perceived control as a reason internal risks may be discounted.

r002.rationale: It describes restricting a productive tool as a difficult organizational decision, but does not identify anticipated staff resentment toward costly safeguards.

r003.rationale: It notes that restricting productive tools is difficult when evidence is uncertain, but does not say staff would consider burdensome safeguards unjustified unless they strongly believed in the risks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one difficulty is that the benefits are very immediate and concrete, whereas the risks are much harder to see. If you deploy a system internally and it makes your researchers more productive, you get feedback on that every day. If it creates a security vulnerability, or starts doing something you didn’t intend, you might not find out until much later. So you can build up a lot of confidence from successful use without actually having tested the thing you’re worried about.

There’s also a slightly misleading intuition that, because it’s internal, it’s controlled. But an internal system might have access to your code, your research, your credentials — precisely the things you most want to protect. The relevant question isn’t just whether outsiders can use it. It’s what permissions it has, what actions it can take, and whether you would notice if something went wrong.

And then there’s the competitive pressure. If you think these systems could substantially accelerate AI research, holding back feels costly. Taking the risks seriously means being willing to limit access or delay deployment even when the productivity gains look very attractive. That’s a much harder organisational commitment than agreeing, in the abstract, that safety matters.

r001.rationale: The response says people may have a misleading intuition that an internal system is controlled, which can lead them to discount its risks.

r002.rationale: It describes competitive pressure and the organizational cost of limiting or delaying deployment, but does not identify anticipated staff resentment toward safeguards.

r003.rationale: It says taking risks seriously may require limiting access or delaying deployment, but does not state that staff will regard burdensome safeguards as justified only if they strongly believe in the risks.
